title: Chemical‐induced aseptic meningitis as a result of intrathecal hydromorphone therapy: Case report
case_prompt: An 81-year-old man with failed back syndrome treated by an intrathecal hydromorphone pump placed three years earlier presented with three days of fever (maximum 38.3 °C) and sudden-onset altered mental status. One week earlier, he had a three-day episode of confusion. He also reported difficulty initiating urination, chronic arthralgia, and intermittent headache. On admission, examination was notable for an exquisitely tender prostate, but urinalysis and blood cultures were negative. Complete blood count showed mild chronic anemia and stable peripheral eosinophilia attributed to seasonal allergies. Empiric ceftriaxone and acetaminophen were started; by hospital day 2 he was afebrile and his mental status normalized. On hospital day 3, he developed acute exacerbation of his chronic back pain and had diffuse tenderness over the lower thoracic spine. MRI of the thoracic and lumbar spine with contrast showed meningeal enhancement in the mid-to-lower thoracic region and possible focal enhancement contacting the intrathecal catheter tip. Ceftriaxone was continued and vancomycin plus ampicillin were added. A lumbar puncture revealed colorless, clear cerebrospinal fluid with 318 nucleated cells/µL (65% eosinophils, 15% neutrophils, 13% lymphocytes), 0 red blood cells, glucose 42 mg/dL (40–70), and protein 135 mg/dL (15–45). CSF PCR assays for bacterial and viral pathogens were negative, and fungal culture showed no growth.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Intrathecal pump catheter infection was considered because of focal contrast enhancement at the catheter tip on MRI — “With concern for intrathecal pump catheter infection or chemical meningitis, a lumbar puncture was ordered…”  
2. Bacterial meningitis was considered given fever, altered mental status, and CSF pleocytosis, but it was excluded since “No viral, bacterial, or fungal cause was found.”  
3. Viral meningitis was considered but excluded when viral PCR assays demonstrated that pathogens were “Not detected.”  
4. Fungal meningitis was considered but excluded because fungal culture showed “No growth.”  
5. Chemical meningitis was favored due to eosinophilic predominance in CSF, elevated protein, normal glucose, and intrathecal hydromorphone exposure, as “The CSF studies were most significant for eosinophilia and elevated CSF protein, making chemical meningitis caused by the hydromorphone via the intrathecal pump the most likely cause.”
